claims.text: A critical nucleation-temperature window exists below the onset of thermal decomposition in rapid thermal synthesis of noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
A moderated heating ramp enables sufficient atomic interdiffusion and homogeneous nucleation.
Sufficient atomic interdiffusion and homogeneous nucleation promote formation of a robust single-phase solid solution.
Ultrafast heating causes abrupt temperature spikes.
Abrupt temperature spikes drive phase separation, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled particle morphology.
Pt-Pd-Au-Ag-Rh-Ir precursor mixtures subjected to standard ultrafast thermal ramps yield nanoparticles with notable phase heterogeneity and elemental segregation.
Changing the thermal ramp profile while holding precursor composition, environment, and final peak temperature constant can test for an optimal nucleation window.
Controlled dwell periods below the thermal-decomposition threshold provide temporal control over the local nucleation temperature.
Temporal control of local nucleation temperature improves nucleation uniformity and minimizes local-overheating-driven phase separation.
A transient thermal plateau permits atomic interdiffusion before critical nucleation is reached.
Pre-nucleation atomic interdiffusion ensures uniform nucleation across the nanoparticle ensemble.
Uniform nucleation suppresses heterogeneous nucleation, phase separation, and elemental segregation.
Relative to ultrafast heating, a moderated ramp will improve single-phase solid-solution crystallinity.
Relative to ultrafast heating, a moderated ramp will produce a more uniform particle-size distribution.
Relative to ultrafast heating, a moderated ramp will reduce elemental segregation.
Traditional ultrafast heating and cooling protocols typically produce phase separation, segregation, and uncontrolled morphology because of abrupt temperature changes.
The proposed mechanism applies near the single-phase formation limit in noble-metal high-entropy alloy systems and when the processing temperature is close to the decomposition onset.
The benefit of a moderated ramp depends on achieving a uniform temperature distribution throughout the sample.
